## HERMETIC PHILOSOPHY
<note>original: "PHILOSOPHIA · HERMETICA". This refers to the ancient tradition of spiritual knowledge attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus, which blends philosophy, alchemy, and theology.</note>

The pedestal is decorated with four red roses and crossed golden rods. Above the pelican, golden sun rays emanate from the top, and the entire central scene is crowned by an Ouroboros <note>the ancient symbol of a serpent biting its own tail, representing the infinite cycle of nature and the unity of the universe</note>.</image-desc>

> There are Two and Three, and yet only One;
> If you do not understand, you will hit upon none,

> From which the whole Work proceeds.
> It is nothing, says the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus"</note>,
> But a double Mercury <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the fluid, transformative principle of matter.</note>.

> Well-being to him who has rightly recognized it.

# Dedicatory Epistle.

)( v

...likewise go further to Vienna, Dresden, and Stuttgart; there they will receive certain news of it. Indeed, if they still do not wish to trust this, they may be informed by the highly learned Mr. **Johann von Horne** <note>Johannes van Horne (1621–1670) was a renowned Dutch anatomist and physician.</note>, the most celebrated Professor of Anatomy and Surgery at the praiseworthy University of Leiden, who wrote to Mr. Dr. Scharduis from the Hague on February 9 of this current year as follows: 

*“What you have heard concerning the <term>Transmutation<note>The alchemical transformation of base metals into gold.</note></term> is all very true; the gold is of the highest proof and most beautiful. Now, therefore, to doubt any further the truth and existence of the art, as well as its practitioners, is madness. They say it was a demon, as if such things were beyond the power of Angels; as if they were not good Angels, or as if gold and medicine were the works of a demon. Shortly, the complete narrative and discussion that Mr. **Schweizerus** <note>Johann Friedrich Schweitzer (1625–1709), also known as Helvetius, a physician who initially doubted alchemy until a mysterious stranger reportedly gave him the means to perform a transmutation in 1666.</note> had with him will be published. This story is spread throughout all Holland, and perhaps all Europe. I rejoice exceedingly that, at last, by such a remarkable experiment, we have been freed from our <term>Thomistic incredulity<note>original: "Thomistica incredulitate." A reference to the biblical "Doubting Thomas," signifying a refusal to believe without direct sensory evidence.</note></term>. The material is a certain mineral, or rather, a **Celestial Salt** <note>original: "Sal cœleste." In alchemical theory, this is a refined, "heavenly" salt seen as the fundamental agent of change.</note>.”* 

And thus far the highly famous Mr. Dr. v[on Horne]...

# Preface
->to the<-
## Kind Reader.

Highly honored and kind, dear reader: those deserve no small amount of praise who highly extol the great and brave heroic deeds of high potentates <note>A "potentate" refers to a person with great power, such as a monarch, ruler, or sovereign.</note>, performed by them in times of both war and peace; who record them in writing and leave them to posterity <note>original: "Nachkömlinge"</note> for eternal memory. Otherwise, if such things were not committed to paper, they would be forgotten; and so, through such forgetfulness, many memorable stories and heroic deeds—indeed, many splendid arts and wonders—would have <note>The text ends here mid-sentence; the truncated word "hät-" is the start of "hätten" (would have), which will conclude the thought on the following page.</note>

...vestigation of such secrets might be refreshed.

Among those excellent men and diligent researchers who have distinguished themselves through their writings in this **century** <note>original: "Seculo"; refers to the 17th century.</note>, one finds **Monsieur de Nuysement** <note>Clovis Hesteau, Sieur de Nuysement (c. 1550–1624), a French poet and alchemist whose works were highly influential in the transmission of Hermetic philosophy.</note>, a **nobleman from Lorraine** <note>original: "Lotharingischer Cavallier"</note>. ## The Author’s Preface. <note>original: "Vorrede des Authoris"</note>

I have no doubt that this book, now brought to light, will be rejected by many and received with gratitude by only a few. For the human intellect—commonly clouded as it is by the fog of ignorance, and because those who see poorly outnumber those with sharp vision—even the higher sciences of knowledge <term>Knowledge (Erkenntnis): in this context, it refers to a deep, often spiritual or philosophical understanding of the world</term> are not esteemed as they deserve. Instead, due to the shameful negligence of people, or a pursuit of profit <note>original: "Gewinsichtigkeit"</note> which always prefers harmful utility over honorable virtue, these sciences lie neglected in contempt. 

Consequently, because some foolishly imagine they were born more for possessing wealth than for seeking knowledge, they surrender themselves entirely to paltry gains. In this, they differ very little from irrational animals and cattle, which look only toward their physical sustenance. If such people were enlightened by the divine ray of knowledge and understanding, they might consider their true status and nature a little more deeply—

<summary>In this preface, the author laments the common human tendency to prioritize material greed and physical survival over intellectual and spiritual enlightenment. He defends the value of the "higher sciences" against a public he expects to be largely ungrateful or indifferent.</summary>

# Of the True Philosophical Salt

### Chapter III.

### That all essential and living things are made through the Spirit of the World, and of the First Matter.

All things are preserved and nourished by that from which they have come; and it is seen that everything that exists breathes, lives, and is nourished by this <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "Spiritum"; refers to the *Spiritus Mundi* or "World Spirit," a vital force believed by alchemists to permeate all matter.</note> implanted in the world, and conversely, where this is lacking, everything dies and decays. Such an essence, however, is in turn spread through all parts of the world, and through it the power and action of the souls are expanded and strengthened; which power is indeed most communicated by those bodies which have drawn somewhat more of this spirit to themselves, and has been poured down from above, namely from the Sun, as that which truly [possesses] the quality (characteristic) of the matter

Therefore, we wish to soar our spirit somewhat higher and more diligently investigate in what manner such things can occur.

# Of the True Philosophical Salt #

...must extract impurities from other things.

> **calcination** was invented for the conquering of hard and stubborn things, specifically because of their cohesion and strong composition, which prevents them from allowing a **separation** <note>original: "separatio"</note> easily unless they are divided into very small pieces.

But yet it is not enough that I have recited this passage from **Ovid** <note>original: "locum Ovidii"; referring to the Roman poet Ovid, whose *Metamorphoses* provided alchemists with many allegories</note>, although according to the secret understanding of the Ancients it is all too true; I wish rather to explain what the Ancients intended to indicate through such a poem, because this is only useful to those experienced in the Art. ### The Author’s Poem <note>original: "Carmen"</note> as the Conclusion of these Books.

Whoever now seeks honor and the fortune of the world in the world,
Let him strive after **Wisdom**, and so he shall find those things;
For **Wisdom** finally leads to the hidden foundations,
And to the peak where, O **Nature**, your treasure is held.
The vain night of error is dispelled through her,
Blind delusion must surely go blind before her light,
The bright light of **Truth** she can kindle in its stead,
So that it pleases her to fetch from the womb of the globe—
Where **Jason** <note>In alchemy, Jason’s quest for the Golden Fleece was often interpreted as an allegory for the search for the Philosopher’s Stone.</note> attained this highly desired prize,
Which, as he then learned, brings healthy blood to the body,
And provides sustenance to one's years, more than he dared hope;
He defied death and laughed at the world's misery,
He was equal to the demigods, having all for which one strives;
Honor and all the fortune of the world stood open to him.

MERCURIUS

### Corollary or Addition.

### At the beginning, the first figure belongs here.

Believe me that the entire company of ancient philosophers kept this greatest secret and mystery most concealed; they never wrote anything about it, nor did they mention this process with a single word.

Therefore, if you read through the books of all the philosophers, you will never find what the **Lili** <term>Lili: A technical alchemical term, often referring to the "white lily" or the purified "prime matter" required for the Great Work</term> signifies, so sparingly have they used its name. Since the time of Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, who was the first beginner of this art, only a single one is to be found who even touched upon the name of the **Lili**: this was the philosopher Haly <note>Likely referring to the Arabic alchemist Haly Abenragel or Khalid ibn Yazid</note> alone.

I have read three more recent philosophers who presented these matters a little more clearly and plainly, among whom Raymond Lully <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a famous polymath and alchemist</note> is the first, of whom it is reported:

*Raymond Lully closes his teachings to no one.* <note>original Latin: "Raymundus Lullius claudens sua dogmata nullis."</note>

->That is:<-

**The philosopher Raymond Lully**
**Feels no displeasure in teaching everyone.**

# CATHOLICON

He [Raymond Lully] uses such words when writing to King Rupert: "O King, you should know that a golden-yellow oil can be made from the **Lead of the Philosophers**: with which—if you sublimate the mineral stone three or four times after its first formation, for three or four days—it will free you from all **dissolution** and **coagulation** <note>In alchemy, "solution" (dissolving) and "coagulation" (solidifying) are the two fundamental processes of the Great Work; the author suggests this oil acts as a shortcut.</note>. The reason is that this hidden oil makes the medicine penetrating, receptive, and cohesive for all bodies, and increases their power beyond measure. Thus, there is nothing more secret in the world than this; therefore, I report wonders to you which all the ancient philosophers would not have believed: namely, that if you knew how to shorten this oil, or to separate it from its wateriness, and to work according to the method of mixture just mentioned, you could make the **Stone** in 30 days."

I therefore often thought to myself what this **Philosophical Lead** might be, for I frequently took it to be of the lineage of **Saturn** <note>Saturn is the traditional alchemical name and planetary correspondence for the metal lead.</note>; but when it came to distillation, it did not work according to my opinion; I therefore sought it much higher.

But finally, fortune willed that I should happen to read **Rupescissa** <note>Johannes de Rupescissa (Jean de Roquetaillade, c. 1310–1366) was a French Franciscan friar whose alchemical writings on the 'quintessence' and medical chemistry were highly influential.</note>, who was a Frenchman; he was the second one who recounted this trade without obscurity, teaching not only me but all who read him. For from him I learned and discovered that a Spanish soldier, through the <term>plumbum Philosophorum</term> <note>original Latin: "Lead of the Philosophers"</note>, understood the <term>Marchafitam plumbeam</term> <note>original Latin: "Leaden Marcasite"; in this era, "marcasite" often referred to various metallic ores or sulfides, such as galena or bismuth, rather than the modern mineral pyrite.</note> to be that which

...who called Rupescissa's **marcasite** <note>original: *marchafitam*. A metallic mineral often confused with pyrite or bismuth in early chemistry; here it is identified with antimony.</note> "Antimony"; he also explains the sayings of Aristotle in the book *The Secret of Secrets* <note>A famous medieval treatise on statecraft and occult sciences attributed to Aristotle.</note>, where he says that this is his "lead," even though he does not call it Antimony by name. This pleased me wonderfully well, and I began to try making it: I dissolved it in distilled vinegar and distilled it, but nothing came of it. But afterward, I learned that it is with *their* vinegar that one draws the **quintessence** <note>original: "q. e." for *quinta essentia*, the "fifth essence" or purest spiritual force within a material.</note> out of Antimony, of which I will speak briefly in the table or the "branches" <note>Likely referring to a diagrammatic tree of alchemical processes.</note>.

Now I come to the third philosopher, namely **Theophrastus Paracelsus**. Upon these three, as well as upon the fourth—namely my own experience—I intend to lay the foundation of this entire structure.

Paracelsus calls Antimony the **Lily of the Ancients**; he also calls it the **Red Lion**. What Rupescissa calls the quintessence, Paracelsus calls the **Blood of the Red Lion**; and when the work has been completed, he calls it the **Physical Tincture** <note>original: *tincturam Physicam*. A medicinal or alchemical solution meant to transform or heal.</note>. (We might also, not unfairly, wish to christen it the "Alchemical Tincture"). Let us therefore proceed to the work with Paracelsus, using his own words: "After I (he says) have sufficiently explained the matter of the Physical Tincture—which could or should hardly be stated more clearly or intimately even between two brothers—let us proceed to the work and the **preparation** <note>original: *præperation*.</note>."

## CATHOLICON

<meta>catchword: Now</meta>

Now, so that we may come to the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The "marriage" or union of the two opposing substances previously prepared.</note>; it is necessary that after the <term>solution</term> <note>The process of dissolving or liquefying the substances.</note> of these two, you take an equal weight of each and place them together in a well-sealed vessel.

After you have put them together, place the glass in the <term>Athanor</term> <note>A self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant, gentle heat over many days.</note>, to <term>putrefy</term> <note>To rot or break down the matter, which alchemists believed was necessary for rebirth.</note> or <term>alter</term> it therein. After 150 days (says <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist.</note>; and I have also found it to be true), as soon as your <term>Lili</term> <note>A term often used by Paracelsus to refer to the purified matter or the "Lily" of the work.</note> in the <term>Philosophical Egg</term> <note>An oval-shaped glass vessel hermetically sealed to ensure no vapor escapes during the long heating process.</note> is warmed, it will appear wondrously, blacker than a raven: then in time whiter than a swan; and finally it passes through yellowing, until it is redder than any blood could be.

This <term>putrefied</term> work, turned into red sulfur, should be considered the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>The ultimate goal of alchemy, capable of transmuting metals and curing disease.</note>; then it is time to <term>ferment</term> <note>To "ripen" the Stone by adding a metallic ferment, usually gold, to give it the "quality" of gold.</note> it.

Of the manner of <term>fermenting</term> it, <term>Paracelsus</term> says this: one should first throw one pound of it onto a thousand pounds of molten gold; then the <term>medicine</term> will be ready to <term>transmute</term> <note>The process of changing base metals into precious ones.</note> the "leprous" metals <note>A common alchemical term for base metals like lead or tin, which were viewed as "diseased" versions of gold.</note>.

This is his <term>fermentation</term> <note>original: *fermentatio*.</note>, which is truly nothing other than his first <term>physical projection</term> <note>The act of casting the finished Stone onto molten metal to effect the transformation.</note>. But if one were to add to this <term>medicine</term> the <term>solution</term> of the red sulfur from the "Red Light" <note>original: *rohten Lumine*. Likely referring to a highly refined tincture or essence.</note> (as is taught in the fourth plate in the book *Of Mercury Reborn* <note>original: *de Mercurio redivivo*. An alchemical text dealing with the restoration and purification of mercury.</note>), so that the spiritual <term>ferment</term> is added to the spiritual Stone; it would be much more penetrating and fluid, just as <term>Paracelsus</term> reports in his *Aurora* <note>original: *aurorâ*. Refers to the *Aurora Thesaurusque Philosophorum* (The Dawn and Treasure of the Philosophers), a work attributed to Paracelsus.</note>.

### Instruction on how one should Calcine Antimony into the Red Lion

Take finely crushed <term>Antimony</term> <note>original: "Antimonium"; a brittle, silvery-gray metalloid that alchemists believed held the secret to the Philosopher's Stone</note>, as much as you wish; add <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>original: "Sal Armoniac"; ammonium chloride, a salt used to help metals melt or react</note> to it, and melt them together in a crucible. When it has melted, pour it quickly into a vessel filled with distilled vinegar, into which you should have previously placed enough of the aforementioned salt. In this way, melt it three times, and always pour it into vinegar at the last. Pour the vinegar off from the <term>Calx of Antimony</term> <note>original: "Antimonii Kalch"; the powdery oxide or "ash" of a metal produced by intense heat</note>, which calx you should dry well and turn into a pure powder, so that you may dissolve it in the manner previously mentioned.

For he who cannot dissolve will also not know how to compose, nor can he ever be a partaker of this science or art.

The ignorance of this Vinegar—about which none of the Ancients have written—has deceived all current laboratory workers; so much so that as long as they lived, they labored for nothing and never understood this Art. Therefore, it is in vain to attempt to make that same Gold, Silver, or <term>potable gold<note>original: aurum potabile; a legendary medicinal liquid thought to contain the essence of gold</note></term>. It is impossible to obtain the Hyle or Chaos of the metals, or the <term>Sulphurs of the lights<note>original: luminum Sulphura; refers to the active internal "souls" or principles of the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver).</note></term>. Many ancient philosophers have spoken of this, among whom Scites is one, who speaks thus in the <note>original: Turba Philosophorum; "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts.</note>*Assembly of the Philosophers*: "All seekers of wisdom should know that the foundation of this Art—for the sake of which many of them have been ruined—is something stronger than all things and higher, yet to the beginners it is easier than all things." By this, he means this Water, to which Pythagoras answered: "O Scites, then name this thing!" Whereupon Scites said: "The sharpest vinegar, which makes gold into pure spirit." Here he speaks of the solution of the

<header>CATHOLICON PHYSICORUM.</header>

...of the red ferment <note>original: fermenti</note>, after which he says—without which neither the manner nor the redness exists—by which words he understands the <term>putrefaction<note>The alchemical stage of decomposition where the matter turns black before it can be reborn.</note></term> of the red light <note>original: luminis</note>. Of this matter Geber <note>An influential 8th-century alchemist, often cited as the father of chemistry.</note> writes thus: by the help of the sharpest vinegar <note>original: Essigs</note>, all kinds of substances are refined and purified; also through distillation, their power and effect are improved. But concerning its composition, neither he nor anyone else has taught, except for the &c. I have no desire to write more of this, nor is it proper; the rest can be whispered into one's ear in secret, or trusted to the artist in my study at Ebrach <note>Referring to the Ebrach Abbey in Bavaria, known for its extensive library and scholarship.</note>, or a good portion of its Milk <note>original: Lactis</note> may be granted, as also concerning the red tincture of Mercury <note>original: Mercurii</note>. And thus, enough has been written so far concerning the Virgin’s Milk or the Philosophical Vinegar.

### The first figure belongs here.

Many have sought the <term>Mineral Stone<note>A specific alchemical substance or stage in the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note></term> in <term>vitriol<note>A sulfate mineral, often iron or copper sulfate.</note></term> or "copper-water," but through their ignorance, they have been entirely deceived and mocked. For common vitriol is only called the "uninformed Green Lion" by the philosophers by way of distinction; but this, our noble <term>Green Lion<note>A key alchemical symbol representing a potent solvent or the raw material of the Great Work, specifically associated here with copper.</note></term>, took its origin from the metallic copper body <note>original: "corpore"</note>. Although an oil can be drawn from <term>Roman Vitriol<note>A high-quality blue vitriol, usually copper sulfate.</note></term>—which is lovelier in scent and more pleasant in taste than any balsam when its tincture is drawn with <term>spirit of wine<note>original: "Sp. vini"; high-proof alcohol or ethanol.</note></term> from the calcined vitriol—the Philosophers nevertheless desire and command that whatever one wishes to use for the <term>transmutation of metals<note>original: "transmutationem metallorum"; the process of turning base metals into gold or silver.</note></term> must proceed from metallic power. Therefore, they teach that such things should be made from bodies <note>original: "ex corporibus"</note>, not from spirits <note>original: "Spiritibus"</note> such as vitriol, sulfur, arsenic <note>original: "Arsenico"</note>, and the like.

Therefore, we find written in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum", one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note> in the first exercise <note>original: "exercitation"</note>: The Philosopher's Stone is a metallic matter <note>original: "Materi"</note> which transforms the essence and substance of metals. However, this transformation or change cannot happen except through its own kind.

### CONVERTED INTO ELIXIR <note>original: "IN ELIXIR CONVERSA"</note>

...which is made in this way, far surpasses the other common vitriols, whether they be Hungarian or Roman <note>These refer to naturally occurring mineral deposits of vitriol named after their regions of origin.</note> which come out of the earth, because it is a physical and metallic vitriol. For otherwise, metallic bodies <note>original: "corpora"</note> could not be transmuted by it. Since, as the <term>Philosopher<note>A general reference to an alchemical authority, often Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus.</note></term> says, everything brings forth its like—namely, that a metallic medicine transmutes metals.

Therefore, says Paracelsus, one should seek in the earth not only the earth itself (which is the vitriol), but the innermost part of the earth, or of the vitriol. By the "innermost of the earth," he meant its sweetness and redness; for within the innermost essence of this vitriol, a subtle, noble, and fragrant juice, or pure oil, lies hidden.

In the preparation of this vitriol, one must primarily take care that this preparation of copper into vitriol is not done through the <term>calcination<note>A process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state, often reducing it to a powder.</note></term> by fire, or through the distillation of the matter, so that it is not robbed of its green color.

Regarding the preparation of this vitriol, Paracelsus says nothing; because of this secrecy, many have erred. We will therefore set this aside for a while and follow the established order of our branch or subject further. We thus begin with the calcination of our metal. However, it must first be noted that this calcination of the copper is done so that it may be turned into a vitriol, and it is not a calcination of the vitriol already made from copper.

# VITRIOLATED VENUS <note>original: "VENUS VITRIOLATA"</note>

Therefore, take as many pounds of thinly beaten copper as you desire and dissolve them in the <term>corrosive water<note>Likely a strong mineral acid such as nitric acid (*aqua fortis*), used to dissolve metallic copper into a solution.</note></term> until the entire matter has dissolved into a clear and green water. Set this to <term>digest<note>A process of gentle, prolonged heating to allow chemical reactions to reach completion.</note></term> for three or four days until the matter is clarified and digested. Pour this into a flask and draw off the corrosive water again, either in warm dung <note>Decomposing manure was used as a source of steady, low heat in alchemical laboratories.</note> or a <term>balneum<note>A water bath or Bain-Marie, used for indirect heating.</note></term>, until the entire substance remains dry behind; thus it is <term>calcined<note>Reduced to a dry powder through the application of heat and the removal of liquid.</note></term>.

Afterward, pour over two pounds of this calcined matter a bottle full of distilled vinegar and seal the glass well. Place it in a hot water bath so that it almost boils, for seven days. When it has cooled down again, pour it into a glass flask and distill all the vinegar over via the water bath; then you will find at the bottom of the flask a coagulated <term>vitriol<note>A metal sulfate; here specifically copper sulfate, prized for its vibrant color and chemical properties.</note></term> much more beautiful than the Roman variety is.

We do not dissolve this vitriol in rainwater, according to the custom of the <term>Paracelsians<note>Followers of the medical and alchemical doctrines of Paracelsus (1493–1541).</note></term>, but rather it should be dissolved in the <term>philosophical vinegar<note>A specialized, highly rectified alchemical solvent, distinct from common table vinegar.</note></term> or in our calcining-water—namely, in the <term>Virgin’s Milk<note>original: "Jungfrau-Milch"; a traditional alchemical term for various white-colored liquid reagents or precipitates.</note></term>—which should be mixed with an equal weight of the corrosive water. After its solution and perfect digestion (namely, after fifteen days), we place it in a flask so that the calcining-water may come away in the water bath. When it has been drawn off, you will find at the bottom of the flask something like an oily water, which will be green, transparent, and clear. This should afterward be strengthened with <term>spirit of wine<note>original: "Spiritu vini"; distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note></term> and again...

### CONVERTED INTO ELIXIR <note>original: "IN ELIXIR CONVERSA."</note>

...grasp; since the **body** <term>corpus<note>The solid, physical remains of the substance.</note></term> is very desirous of its **soul** <term>anima<note>The volatile essence or "tincture" that carries the transformative properties.</note></term>, and the soul also delights in embracing its body.

However, so that they may be converted into a **stone** <note>original: "lapidem"</note>, place this composite matter into the secret furnace, namely the **Athanor** <term>Athanor<note>A self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a uniform, constant heat over long periods, essential for the "slow cooking" of alchemical digestion.</note></term>, for 40 days. When the stone has been prepared in this way, we come to its fermentation, without which it is impossible to give it a form; thus, we must not follow the teaching of a single person against the entire **Assembly of Philosophers** <note>original: "Turbam Philosophorum." For they have all concluded that one must necessarily give the stone a form through the **ferment** <note>original: "fermentum"</note>, and that the **Elixir** is not made without the **conjunction** or union of two bodies: namely, the stone, which is made from the imperfect body, and the ferment from the perfect one. And the more spiritual the ferment is, the greater the effect and penetrating power, as well as the **transmutation**, the stone would have. 

Since you have thus been taught by these **precepts** <note>original: "præceptis"</note>, we hold no other views than those who proceed to projection instead of fermentation, or that the **stone** <note>original: "Lapis"</note> in this way with the corporeal gold, which is not altered, fermenti-

### Addition.

Enough has been mentioned in the previous book regarding the **purification** <note>original: "purgation"</note> and **cleansing** <note>original: "depuration"</note> of **Mercury** <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note>. Therefore, it remains for us to also say something about the cleaning of **Lead** and **Tin**.

Therefore, let the lead melt in a **crucible** <term>crucible<note>A ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at very high temperatures.</note></term>; and when you see that it flows, let it stand thus in the fire for a quarter of an hour. Afterward, throw a little **Sal ammoniac** <term>Sal ammoniac<note>original: "Sal armoniacum" (ammonium chloride), used in alchemy as a flux to clean the surface of molten metal by reacting with oxides.</note></term> onto the lead; let it stand a while longer in the fire, and stir the lead around with an iron wire until the Sal ammoniac has gone off in smoke. Remove the impurities that float on the crucible; then let the lead cool, and it will be as white as **Silver**.

In this way, you can purify your lead or tin before you perform the **projection** <term>projection<note>The final step of the alchemical process where the "Stone" or "Elixir" is cast onto a molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note></term>, because no other **bodies** <note>original: "corpora," referring to the physical forms of the metals.</note> or **metals** <note>original: "metalla"</note> are as fluid and suitable for projection as these. For this reason, one must project every Elixir—to make or transmute metals—upon Mercury, or upon Lead or Tin.

### The first figure belongs here.

Although the <term>liquids of the Moon and Sun</term> <note>original Latin: "liquores Lunæ und Solis." In alchemical symbolism, the Moon represents Silver and the Sun represents Gold.</note>, namely of gold and silver, can be called **Potable Gold** and **Potable Silver** <note>original: "Aurum und Argentum potabile." These were liquid medicines made from noble metals, believed to have near-miraculous healing powers.</note>—if they have first stood in the digestion of the <term>Water-bath</term> <note>original: "Balnei" (Bain-marie), a method of gentle heating by placing a vessel in hot water.</note> for one or seven days with pure rectified **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: "Spir. vini," or high-proof alcohol, used as a solvent.</note> poured over the dissolved liquid, and then drawn off again through the helm <note>The "helm" or alembic is the top part of a still where vapors condense and are funneled into a receiver.</note> so that the solutions or oils remain behind, and can then safely be given to the body as good medicines—the Philosophers nevertheless prefer it otherwise. For they desire and teach that metals should first be brought into the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>original: "Q. E." or "Quinta Essentia." The "fifth element," thought to be the purest and most potent medicinal core of a substance.</note> before they are consumed internally by mouth; also, that there are no true Quintessences except those of the <term>second nature</term> <note>In alchemy, a substance of the "second nature" is one that has been transformed from its raw state into a higher, more active philosophical state.</note>, according to the old saying:

> **The Elixir is by its nature a second thing,** <note>original Latin: "Elixir de se est res secunda"</note>
> **From which pure bodies are made:** <note>original Latin: "De quo sunt facta corpora munda"</note>

Namely, that the four Elements must first be broken down, and a new body made through <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The process of "rotting" or decomposition in alchemy, which was seen as a necessary stage of death before a substance could be reborn in a purified form.</note>, and thus the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> is brought about; which, as it pleased **Ripley** <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist and author of *The Compound of Alchemy*.</note> to say, is the Quintessence. I, however, may briefly affirm that no true potable gold or silver...

# ELIXIR

...nor can the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>original: "Q. E." or "Quinta Essentia," the purest medicinal core of a substance.</note> be made unless it first becomes an **Elixir**. Now that we are speaking more fully of these Elixirs, or medicines of life, it should be known that **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, when he speaks of <term>fermentation</term> <note>A process where the alchemical medicine is "seeded" with the qualities of a specific metal.</note>, commands one to take Gold or its **Shadow**. Silver does not become bright except through the radiance of the Sun <note>The Sun is the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note>. One must therefore first speak of the <term>body</term> <note>original Latin: "corpore." Indeed, concerning Gold, it is written thus in the books of the **Chymical Art**: The **Philosopher’s Stone** is made from Gold alone and from nature alone; and that same stone is superior, for it is said by the Philosophers that it shall cure all diseases.

Thus, according to the opinion of this Philosopher, we have decided to begin with Gold alone: the medicine which is the ancient and healthy Quintessence. However, so that this Gold may become better and purer, it can be purified in two ways: namely through **Antimony**, so that it is cast through in the manner that goldsmiths do, until the gold on the bottom is beautiful, pure, and clear, and free from the addition and [impurity] <note>The original text cuts off here; the catchword "Unraht" (dross/impurity) indicates the next page's beginning.</note> of other metals.

Its nature is of much heat, yet tempered; for it has many properties and virtues: it cleanses the body of diseases that have occurred and preserves it in a healthy state, so that no adversities or destructions appear or are seen, nor any loosening of its bond; that is, the life of the dead and their resurrection, a medicine that preserves the body and cleanses away excess <note>"Superfluity" refers to the imbalance of bodily humors (fluids) which pre-modern doctors believed caused sickness.</note>.

**Robertus Vallensis** <note>Robert Duval (c. 1490–1567), a French alchemist and scholar who wrote early histories of alchemical practice.</note> recounts at length: the **Elixir**, or the **medicine of life**, or the **potable gold** <note>original: "Aurum potabile"; a legendary alchemical remedy consisting of gold dissolved into a liquid state, believed to grant longevity.</note>, as you may wish to call it, truly has a wondrous power: for it heals every person, whether they be sick internally or externally, in a very short time; because it restores the elements themselves—which proceed from their natural **symmetry** <note>original: "Symmetriâ"; referring to the ideal balance or proportion of the bodily humors.</note>—and brings their weakened actions and **sinning humors** <note>original: "peccirende Feuchtigkeiten"; in traditional medicine, these were bodily fluids that had become unbalanced or "corrupt," leading to disease.</note> back to their proper nature. 

For it is an incorruptible work, tempered, purified, and separated from the **dregs** <note>original: "fecibus"; the impurities or waste matter.</note> of the four elements, which are the primary cause of **corruption** <note>original: "corruption"; the process of physical decay and aging.</note>. Therefore, it makes the body temperate and healthy, just like the spirit of life, by whose power and help nature digests the indigestible and expels all that is undigested; it cuts away all superfluous and sinning qualities, revives the spirit, makes the soft hard and the hard soft, the thin thick and the lean fat, consumes the [excess] fat, cools what is hot and heats what is cold, dries the moist and moistens the dry; it [restores] the natural heat or the **substantial moisture** <note>original: "humidum substanticum"; the essential, life-sustaining fluid within the body, also known as radical moisture.</note>...

### The first figure belongs here.

Although many have written about <term>Saturn<note>In alchemy, Saturn is the traditional name for the metal lead. It also represents the "Nigredo" or black stage—the initial, heavy phase of the alchemical process.</note></term>, they have done so only in fragments here and there. No one has yet produced anything whole or complete. We, however, intend not only to set down truthfully and as briefly as possible that which we have gathered and transcribed from others but also to record what we have discovered through our own experience, so that this may be an absolute and perfect work.

Concerning this, <term>Maria<note>Known as Maria Prophetissa or Mary the Jewess, she was a legendary foundational figure in alchemy, historically credited with the invention of several types of chemical apparatus, including the double-boiler or "bain-marie."</note></term>—who, as they say, was the prophetess and sister of Moses—is read to have written the following in her book on the **Work of Saturn** <note>original: "opere Saturni"</note>: "Make your running water like the water from two <term>Zaibeths<note>An alchemical term of Arabic origin usually referring to types of mercury or quicksilver.</note></term> prepared by God, and fix it over the fixed heart of Saturn. And then also marry the <term>gum<note>original: "gummi." In alchemical texts, "gum" often refers to a semi-solid, resinous state of matter during the transformation of minerals.</note></term> with the gum, as in a true **marriage**, and ensure that it becomes like a running water." Regarding this process of Maria’s, our own George Ripley speaks thus in the *Verses of Genius* <note>original: "Carminibus Genialibus"</note> of his book:

> Maria speaks of wondrous things,
> And gives us gifts of great worth;
> With two gums she fixes the one
> Who wears the wings upon his hat. <note>The figure with wings on his hat is Mercury (the god Hermes), symbolizing volatile quicksilver. "Fixing" him means turning a liquid or gas into a solid state.</note>

# DISSOLVED
<note>original: "DISSOLUTUS"</note>

...packed <note>This completes the word from the previous page's catchword "cke," likely "gepacket" (packed or placed).</note>; which should be done in a stone jug with a narrow neck: this should be placed in warm ashes until it has completely **dissolved** <note>original: "solviret"</note> and the material at the bottom of the glass is white, like small white grains of salt, which is a sign of its total dissolution. Then pour the dissolved material, along with the water, into a small flask <note>original: "Kölblein"</note> and place an **alembic** <note>original: "Helm;" the cap or "helmet" of a still used to collect and direct vapors during distillation.</note> upon it, and draw off the water in a **water bath** <note>original: "Balneo," referring to the *balneum Mariae*, a vessel of hot water used for gentle, even heating.</note> until the material remains dry in the flask; thus you will have turned the **body** <note>original: "corpus"</note> into a white powder through the **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter and reduce it to a powder.</note> of the corrosive water, from which the **Heart of Saturn** <note>original: "Hertz Saturni." In this context, it refers to the purified essence or "salt" of lead.</note> may thereafter be drawn off.

Then wash or purify the corrosive water from your white body in this manner: pour warm water onto this remaining substance in the flask and **extract** <note>original: "extrahirs"</note> it repeatedly until you find it pleasant on the tongue and free of all sharpness. Then this body is prepared for its salt to be extracted from it.

In the writings of Isaac <note>likely Isaac Hollandus, a 15th-century alchemist known for his work on lead</note>, a method is found to extract the mercury from Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for the metal Lead</note>: from which I, using his "Paradise Water," know how to prepare a special shortcut. ### To this place belongs the second figure.

Our Thomas Norton <note>Thomas Norton (c. 1433–c. 1513) was an English alchemist and author of the famous poem *The Ordinal of Alchemy*</note> speaks thus in one place in his writings: the alchemists know how to make running mercury <term>Mercurium currentem: liquid quicksilver</term> out of lead through an easy art. However, what that same art was, neither he nor any of the ancients has shown us, nor have they taught the method <note>original: "modum"</note> of the practice. Search, search, says the highest spagyrist <term>Spagyrus: a practitioner of spagyric medicine, which involves the alchemical separation and recombination of natural substances</term> (which Paracelsus <note>a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals in medicine</note> also commands), and you will find; knock and it shall be opened to you—which are more the words of an envious person <note>Alchemists often called those who hid their secrets "envious" or "stingy"</note> than the precepts <note>original: "præcepta"</note> of a teaching master. 

But since I have been so instructed, I have learned to search, which is to say, to read; when I had read, I knocked, which is to say, I tried the experiments <note>original: "experimenta"</note>; although some were contrary to philosophy <note>original: "Philosophiæ"</note>. And although I had almost despaired of this art—of searching for or finding such a thing—yet because nothing is too difficult for a diligent and industrious student, I have finally found the opening through frequent knocking. Through this, I learned this easy art, namely the method <note>original: "modum"</note> to make living silver <term>argentum vivum: quicksilver or mercury</term> out of lead. This process is such that, when it is read by the laborer <note>original: "Laboranten": the person performing the manual work in the laboratory</note>, it is more likely to be despised by him than believed.

This **Spirit** is indeed the **Air of the Stone** <note>original: "des Steins Lufft"</note> and is purified in the seventh distillation, always removing its water. This **Spirit**, thus prepared, must be kept in a well-sealed glass in a cool place so that its scent does not evaporate. For in this step, you have separated and purified the **first element** <note>original: "primum elementum"</note>, namely the **Air**, the **Spirit**, or the **white tincture**.

When you have thus well-purified the **Air** or **Spirit**, let the flow or the water evaporate <note>original: "exhaliren oder verrauchen"</note> in this same **water bath** <note>original: "Balneo"</note>, yet with a strong degree of fire. This water does not look like the **Air**, but is instead whitish; and once it has risen over the **distillation head** <note>original: "Helm" — the top part of an alembic or still</note>, the material at the bottom remains cloudy, which still contains the remaining two elements, namely **Fire** and **Earth**.

Upon this **thick matter**, pour your distilled water, and drive the water or **Oil** out in a stronger degree of **ash heat** <note>original: "grad der Aschen" — a sand or ash bath provides a more intense, even heat than a water bath</note>. This must be distilled three times until you have purified it; this is the **Fire of the Stone**, the **Soul** <note>original: "anima"</note>, and also the **red tincture**.

<summary>This page details the extraction of the "Spirit" or "Air" from the Sericon and the subsequent separation of the "Water" and "Fire" (the Soul) through varying degrees of heat.</summary>

The alchemical process, taught with the unanimous consensus of the philosophers, as he says. What does he mean by the **Daughter of Pluto**? He reveals this in another place and calls it the **Sulfur of Nature** <note>original: "Sulphur naturæ"</note>.

# The Riplæan Abridgement of Sublimated Mercury, expanded and improved.
<note>Referencing George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist whose works were highly influential in 16th and 17th-century Germany.</note>

You, my dear fellow-laborer! Whoever you may be, who desires to assist and serve yourself in these things at your own expense; read through Ripley’s *Medulla* <note>original: "Medullam"; likely referring to Ripley's "Medulla Alchimiae" or "The Marrow of Alchemy."</note>, and endeavor to perform his "abridgement" <term>Abridgement: A shortened or simplified alchemical process.</term> of **sublimated mercury** <term>Sublimated mercury: Mercuric chloride, a highly toxic and corrosive white crystalline powder used as a primary material in alchemical works.</term>; which, in order that it may pass from the abridgement into the Greater Elixir, I will help you by adding more information. Therefore, take one pound of sublimated mercury and sublime it again by itself six times. After that, you shall prepare a half-ounce <note>original: "Loth"; a historical German unit of weight, roughly 15-16 grams.</note> of gold by means of **antimony** <term>Antimony: A semi-metal used in alchemy to purify gold, as it eats away base metals, leaving the "pure" gold behind.</term>, and file it very small. You shall dissolve this in the corrosive water <note>Likely aqua regia or a similar strong acid.</note> strengthened with **sal ammoniac** <term>Sal ammoniac: Ammonium chloride, often used to increase the potency of acids to allow them to dissolve gold.</term>. To this, add an equal weight of our sharpest vinegar, or **Virgin's Milk** <note>original: "Lactis virginis"; an alchemical term for a white, cloudy liquid or a specific potent solvent.</note>, and let it stand thus in the **water bath** <note>original: "Balneo"; a Bain-marie or heated vessel of water used for gentle, even heating.</note> for seven days.

Then distill the dissolving-water away from the gold, and onto the oil that remains at the bottom, pour distilled vinegar; in its redness you will see several little sparks of gold. Draw the vinegar off from it and dry the material well, then dissolve it anew with fresh dissolving-water. Distill it once more so that the gold is entirely turned into an oil and remains behind.

<summary>This page provides a refined laboratory procedure based on George Ripley’s "abridgement," detailing the purification of mercury and the transformation of gold into a medicinal "oil."</summary>

**Then**, take one and a half ounces of your **sublimate** <term>Sublimate: Mercuric chloride, prepared in the previous steps.</term> and **wax it** <term>Wax it (Inceration): To mix a liquid or "oil" into a dry substance over heat until it reaches a waxy, non-volatile consistency.</term> with your **dissolved gold** <note>original: "solvirten Gold"; gold previously brought into a liquid state via acid.</note> in a glass vessel, which must be sealed in the best possible way. Afterward, **dissolve** one part of your gold—thus transmuted and turned to powder through the **projection** <term>Projection: The final stage of the Great Work, where the Medicine is cast upon a base metal to transform it into gold, or in this case, upon gold to "multiply" the medicine's power.</term>—with distilled vinegar into an oil. Then take the third part of your withheld medicine and dissolve it likewise with vinegar, and pour both solutions together.

# THE COMPLETION OF ALCHEMY

...preparing, fermenting into an <term>Elixir</term> <note>A potent alchemical substance capable of transmuting metals or healing illness.</note>, and augmenting in power or in quantity, is but a single Philosophical Work, of which the entire <term>Assembly of Philosophers</term> <note>original: "turba Philosophorum." This refers to an ancient alchemical text depicting a gathering of sages, often cited as a collective authority.</note> has written constantly, without ceasing, forever and always.

However, the distinct <term>method</term> <note>original: "modus."</note> of operating in this Art is well worth noting; for example: the production, or the creation of the white sulfur, is always performed in the <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "Balneo." Specifically a "balneum Mariae," a gentle heating method using a double boiler.</note>; but its reddening occurs in the <term>ash bath</term> <note>original: "Aschen." A sand or ash bath allows for higher, more even temperatures than water.</note>; and so it is with many others.

Therefore, in all alchemical works, it is necessary that the artist understands well and subtly the difference and distinction of Nature, as well as of Art, and what belongs to each.

To Nature belongs the natural <term>Archaeus</term> <note>original: "Archæus." In the tradition of Paracelsus, this is the "inner alchemist" or vital force that directs the growth and maturation of all things.</note> as well as the <term>mineral cycle</term> <note>original: "mineralium periodus."</note>, through which it allows metals to grow in the womb of the earth from an imperfect and impure <term>Mercury</term> and from an imperfect and impure <term>Sulfur</term>, according to whether they are pure or impure. In the greater heat of the climate, the Sun and the Moon—namely gold and silver—are formed; likewise in cold climates, the other five <term>imperfect bodies</term> <note>The base metals: lead, tin, iron, copper, and mercury.</note> are produced, according to the variety or alternation of each climate, and the place and property, as well as the degree of heat. To bring this <term>projection</term> <note>The final stage of the Great Work where the alchemist "throws" the Stone or elixir onto base metal to trigger transmutation.</note> to its conclusion, the process shall be, according to the opinion of **Arnold** <note>Arnold de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note> from the second book of his **Rosary** <note>original: *Rosarii* (Rosarium Philosophorum), one of the most famous medieval alchemical treatises.</note> in the 31st Chapter: he commands projecting one part of the corporeal <term>elixir</term> onto one hundred parts of purified and washed <term>mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurii*.</note>, and that will all become the medicine. After that, project one part of this latter congealed <note>solidified</note> medicine onto another hundred parts of purified <term>mercury</term>, and all of it will become gold and silver, perfect and pure, according to whether the first <term>elixir</term> had been <term>prepared</term> and <term>composed</term> as white or red <note>White elixirs were used to create silver, while red elixirs were for gold.</note>.

Finally, to briefly repeat this completed <term>method</term> of <term>projection</term>: first, the <term>medicines</term> should be projected onto their <term>ferments</term> <note>Substances—usually pure gold or silver—added to the Stone to "fix" its power and give it a specific "metallic" direction.</note>; then onto molten gold or silver; after that onto mercury until they transform it into the medicine; and lastly onto the closer metals <note>original: *nähern Metallen*. These are "base" metals like lead or tin, which were thought to be chemically "near" to mercury.</note>, so that they are changed into good gold and silver, according to the property and <term>quality</term> of the medicine.

Because we have spoken of the <term>proximity</term> <note>original: *propinquität*.</note> and affinity of the metals—namely, that the <term>elixir</term> is to be projected upon the <term>imperfect body</term> <note>original: *imperfecte corpus*. A base metal that has not yet reached the "perfected" state of gold.</note> from which its <term>mercury</term> and <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury and Sulfur are the two primary principles or "parents" of all metals.</note> were previously extracted—we will here propose an example: if the medicine were made from <term>mercury</term>, it should then be projected onto mercury to become gold or silver, because mercury is the <term>body</term> closest to <term>mercury</term>. And the same applies to the others.

# COMPLETION OF ALCHEMY.

Divide your white sulfur <note>original: "Schweffel"; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of matter.</note> thus prepared into two parts; keep one for the **White Stone** <note>The stage of the Philosopher’s Stone capable of transmuting metals into silver.</note> and make the other red for the **Red Work** <note>The final, most potent stage of the Great Work, used to produce gold and the elixir of life.</note>. In this way, you will have your two minerals <note>original: "mineras"</note> of which it is said: "Our metals are nothing other than our two minerals of our Sun and Moon" <note>original: "Solis und Lunæ"; alchemical code for Gold and Silver.</note>, as Raymond <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy.</note> has wisely recorded, and so forth until the end of the verses <note>original: "carminum"; referring to alchemical poems or instructional songs.</note>. Now you have your two prepared sulfurs. If you are a **Philosopher** <note>A "Philosopher" in these texts refers specifically to a master of alchemy.</note>, then proceed to the end and conclude the work in the tenth number <note>A reference to the Pythagorean idea of ten as the number of perfection and completion.</note>, and give the sulfur its **Mercury** <note>The passive, fluid, and feminine principle required to balance the sulfur.</note> so that the task is finished. If not, then you were not born for our philosophy.

**Note:** That the Sulfur of the Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophorum Schweffel"</note> is not the common mineral sulfur from which metals grow under the earth. Rather, it is the purified sulfur drawn out from the metals through the Art <note>The "Art" is the standard term used by practitioners to describe the alchemical process.</note> and brought to the surface, from which—and from the mercury of the body <note>original: "corporis Mercurio"</note>—the Stone arises.

# AND PERFECTION.

...meant; although it pleased Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed.</note> to say and testify that no one had ever taught or prophesied anything of this Art except at the danger of his soul, as if he had received a gift of trust and faith from the Author of Faith <note>A reference to God as the source of all true wisdom.</note>, so that he might leave it to the faithful. Yet, when you read his writings, whether it be his **Emerald Tablet** <note>original: "Schmaragd-Tafel"; a brief, cryptic text highly revered by alchemists as the foundation of their art.</note>, or his **Apocalypse**, or the **Twelve Golden Chapters**, you will find just as little that is openly revealed. What, my dear friend, are you to think of such an author?

Believe me, all the ancients have hidden the secrets of the preparation in the "gross work" <note>The physical, material manipulation of substances as opposed to the purely spiritual aspect.</note>; although they have written abundantly about the philosophical [side]. Therefore, we have applied diligence to learn this, for we have found from their books that the **Elixir** <note>The medicinal or transmutative substance sought by alchemists.</note> can be made from the planets or metals <note>In alchemical code, the "planets" refer to the seven metals: Sun/Gold, Moon/Silver, Mars/Iron, etc.</note>, and also from the intermediate minerals <note>original: "minerals"; substances like antimony or vitriol that were seen as not yet fully matured into metals.</note> which incline more toward the metallic nature. Afterward, we read further and discovered a method <note>original: "Methodum"</note> among them all, which they pointed toward with a single mind, heart, and opinion, in this manner:

First and foremost, that the bodies <note>original: "corpora"; the solid metallic materials.</note> should be brought to bodies, meaning that they should be disincorporated or decomposed and brought into a liquid <note>original: "liquorem"</note> which they have named **Hyle** <note>A Greek term for primordial, unformed matter.</note> or **Chaos**.

Secondly, that from the chaotic substance, which is nonetheless a single thing, the **three elements** <note>In this context, likely referring to the "Tria Prima" or Three Primes: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> should be separated and purified.

Thirdly, that the separated and purified elements <note>original: "Elementa"</note> would be joined—the man and the woman, heaven and earth—and thus referred to by countless names so that the ignorant might think they were different things. In truth, this was nothing other than water and salt, the white or red mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, and earth. These they unified at once so that, in the process of decay <note>original: "putrefaction"; the essential alchemical stage where the substance decomposes and turns black before its "rebirth."</note>, a new and pure body would be created according to the pattern of Creation, namely the microcosmic child or the sulfur of nature <note>original: "Sulphur naturæ"; the active, spiritual seed or "fire" within a substance.</note>.

Fourthly, that it would be fed with milk and then nourished and maintained through fermentation, so that it might grow to its perfect strength.

Since we have now taught this, we proceed to the practice <note>original: "practic"</note>. In the practice of every body <note>original: "corporis"</note> or spirit, we find various errors; but as we read more and experiment more, we have finally discovered the method <note>original: "modum"</note> to dissolve, separate, and unite all bodies. We found their composition from the most secret of secrets: namely, the **Virgin’s Milk** <note>original: "Lactis virginis"; a cryptic term for a white, potent solvent or a specific state of the mercurial water.</note>, or the **sharpest vinegar** <note>original: "aceti acerrimi"; often referring to a highly rectified acidic spirit used in dissolution.</note>, and Raymond’s <note>Likely referring to the works of Pseudo-Ramon Llull, a legendary figure in alchemy associated with the use of potent solvents and "waters."</note> calcining water. With these, we dissolved all bodies as we pleased and completed the gross work <note>original: "opus grossum"; the physical laboratory operations of handling and purifying materials.</note>.

Therefore, we have decided, contrary to the usual philosophical custom <note>Alchemists typically swore oaths of secrecy; the author here claims to be breaking that tradition for the benefit of the reader.</note>, to reveal the entire work <note>original: "opus"</note>, so that we might not be a cause of error for those who might envy us. Thus, we have added to that which is ours, which was...

<meta>This page continues the previous discussion by providing a systematic list of the specific operations required to prepare "imperfect bodies" into the final Elixir. It translates the general "Tree" concept into nine practical steps.</meta>

->### THE COMPLETION OF ALCHEMY ###<-

<meta>catchword: And</meta>

# The mode or manner / way and type / of preparing the imperfect bodies. <note>original: "unvollkommene corpora"; the "imperfect bodies" usually refer to base metals like lead or iron that the alchemist intends to purify and transmute into gold or silver.</note>

1. <term>Calcination</term> of bodies, or the reduction of the bodies to ash. <note>original: "Calcinatio corporum"; the process of heating a substance in an open crucible until it is reduced to a fine powder or "ash."</note>
2. <term>Dissolution</term> into <term>Hyle</term>, or the opening up into Hyle. <note>original: "Solutio in Hylen"; Hyle is a term derived from Greek meaning "prime matter"—the fundamental, undifferentiated substance from which all physical things are formed.</note>
3. Separation of the Hyle through <term>distillation</term>, or the parting of the Hyle through distillation. <note>original: "Separatio Hyles per destillationem"</note>
4. <term>Conjunction</term> of the separated parts for <term>putrefaction</term>, or the union of the separated elements for rotting. <note>original: "Conjunctio seperatorum ad putrefactionem"; putrefaction was seen as a necessary stage of decay that allowed for new life or higher forms to emerge.</note>
5. Putrefaction of the united parts into <term>Sulfur</term>, or the rotting of the joined elements into Sulfur. <note>original: "Putrefactio conjunctorum ad Sulphurem"; in this context, "Sulfur" refers to the combustible, oily, and "soul" principle of the material, not just the chemical element.</note>
6. Preparation of the Sulfur for <term>fermentation</term>, or the preparation of the Sulfur to ferment. <note>original: "Sulphuris præparatio ad fermentation"</note>
7. Fermentation for the <term>Elixir</term>, or fermenting into the Elixir. <note>original: "Fermentatio ad Elixir"; the Elixir is the perfected alchemical substance, often synonymous with the Philosopher's Stone in its liquid or medicinal form.</note>
8. <term>Augmentation</term> of the Elixir in virtue, or the multiplication of the Elixir’s strength, virtue, and effect. <note>original: "Elixiris augmentatio in virtute"</note>
9. Augmentation of the Elixir in quantity through <term>projection</term>, or the multiplication of the Elixir’s size through projection. <note>original: "Elixiris augm. in quantitate per projectionem"; projection is the final act of casting a small amount of the Elixir onto a large mass of molten base metal to transform it into gold.</note>

Some establish twelve parts; but the other three grades <note>original: "gradus"</note> are comprised under these.

Here are found branches from the Tree of Knowledge, branches of health, and branches of all the abundance of the Sun and the Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun and Moon represent Gold and Silver, the two "perfect" metals.</note>, namely of gold and silver; here spring forth the finest little streams of science and knowledge, which are artfully prepared throughout the garden, flowing over the most precious noble stones, and even over the sand of gold and silver. Therefore we should thank God at all times for His wondrous gifts; we should honor Him, obey Him, love Him, and also pray to Him that He might rule over us with His grace and lead us into eternity through all His paths of goodness, knowledge, and faith, into eternal life, Amen.

# Interpretation of Obscure Words and Speeches

-><image-desc>A decorative horizontal band of typographic ornaments consisting of repeating floral and cross-like motifs arranged in three rows.</image-desc><-

So that the sayings <note>original: "dicta"</note>, proverbs, and speeches of the ancient sages—which are all too obscure and darkened—might be understood, one must first consider their manifold meanings. This is so that the good-hearted reader may know exactly how the ancients wished one thing or another to be understood. Otherwise, there would arise a confusion, muddle, and darkness of understanding and of knowledge in this **Divine Art**. <note>The "Divine Art" refers to Alchemy, which practitioners believed was a gift from God to humanity.</note> To ensure that such confusion is cleared away, I have deemed it fair and good to describe this useful **little treatise** <note>original: "Tractätlein"</note> regarding the study of ancient writings. In the first part, the manifold considerations of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii." In alchemy, "Mercury" often refers to a philosophical principle rather than the common liquid metal.</note> shall be treated.

1. Therefore, one must mark and take note that when the **Philosophers** speak of **Mercury**, it is not the common quicksilver, but rather the **sublimate**. <note>A "sublimate" is a substance produced when a solid is heated into a vapor and then collected again as a solid, usually used here to mean a purified chemical state.</note>

2. In the second consideration, it is taken for the **calcining water**, which dissolves all **bodies**. <note>original: "corpora." In this context, "bodies" refers to solid metals or minerals. "Calcining water" usually refers to a strong acid or corrosive solvent used to break down these materials.</note>

3. In the third, it is taken for the **Mercury** of any **body**, that is, for the **white tincture** of the body. <note>The "white tincture" is a specific stage in the alchemical process, often associated with the ability to transmute base metals into silver.</note>

1. As one then finds in *The Sound of the Trumpet* <note>original: "Clangore Buccinæ," a well-known alchemical treatise likely of 16th-century origin</note>: **Mercury** is a tincture <note>A substance capable of permeating and changing the color or nature of a metal</note> or a permanent water, extracted from the bodies through dissolution or melting, and through sublimation and refinement.

2. In this, the Philosophers did not mean the quicksilver nor the Mercury that one sees [with the eyes], nor the Magnesia that one beholds; rather, by Mercury, they understood the moisture of that same mixture, which is the **radical moisture** <note>original: "humiditas radicalis," the fundamental, innate moisture believed to be the life-force within matter</note>, the basic wetness of our **Stone**. <note>The "Stone" refers to the Philosophers' Stone, the ultimate goal of the alchemical process.</note>

**Senior** <note>Refers to Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umail</note> also speaks of this same Mercury; he takes quicksilver for Mercury (which often happens and is used as such), for he says: quicksilver is a **Spirit**, and it is called the "permanent water," or the "vinegar," or the **solvent** <note>original: "menstruum," here meaning a solvent used to dissolve solids, not the biological term</note>, or the **nourishment** <note>original: "nutriment"</note>

There are four kinds of **calcination** in our Work:
1. First, in the **preparation** of the Work, the **reduction of the body** to **lime** <note>original: "Kalch" or calx; the powdery residue left after a metal is burned</note> through fire is considered.

4. Fourth, it refers to the dry parts after **putrefaction**, when they are **coagulated** <term>coaguliret; the thickening of a liquid into a solid</term> into powder.

**Solution** is fivefold: namely, the Main Solution; the **solution** of the elements; the Philosophical **solution**; the **solution** of the **ferment** <term>the substance that triggers a transformation in the chemical mass, much like yeast in dough</term>; and the **solution** of the Stone and the **Elixir**.

1. The Main Solution is a **reduction** of the imperfect **body** <note>original: "corporis"</note> into a **liquid** <note>original: "liquorem"</note> or **Chaos** <term>a primal, undifferentiated state of matter</term>.

2. The **solution** of the elements is a **separation** or parting from its **Chaos** through distillation into the elements: namely, into **Mercury**, **Sulfur**, and **Salt**; or into **Spirit**, **Soul**, and **Body**; or into **Water**, **Fire** (or **Oil**), and **Earth**.

Thus, my dear reader, you are sufficiently instructed by this; you can boldly explore the books of all the philosophers with good understanding.

### Chapter II.

## Of Nature and of Art.

Now, however, in this snail-round world <note>original: "Schnecken-runden Welt"; a poetic Renaissance description of the spherical cosmos or the winding complexity of the natural world</note>, there are two working causes: Nature and Art. <note>In alchemical texts, "Art" refers to the "Great Work" of human skill and chemical intervention.</note>

Nature produces and brings forth new things daily. But Art, which strongly envisions the uniformity of those things through a defined pattern, mimics Nature's designs, as it were, "on her very heels" <note>original: "auf der Fussocken," literally "on the foot-socks"; an idiom meaning to follow closely or imitate immediately</note> in a wonderful way. However, it is so that if human wit and understanding did not come to the aid of certain things, it is clear and obvious that Nature herself could not reach her full effect and completion. For Art, with the assistance of Nature, occasionally improves, completes, and repairs Nature; and by all appearances, in some measure—especially in this generous effort and labor—it far surpasses the mineral ore-mines <term>mineralische Fund-gruben: refers to the natural deposits of metals in the earth, which the alchemist seeks to replicate or improve upon in the laboratory</term>; as has long since been left behind by the ancient philosophers in memorable writings.

### An explanation of why the Philosophers kept this science hidden; wherein the Art is given its praise, and its detractors are addressed.

But as to why the Philosophers left this art to posterity and to those devoted to wisdom through parables—which carry great weight behind them—and dark riddles; one called **Hamel** (or Hanil) <note>Likely a corruption of "Ibn Umail," the 10th-century Arabic alchemist known in Latin as **Senior Zadith**.</note>, in his treatise which he titled **The Elder** <note>original: "Seniorem." ...therefore, by necessity, a conflict or discord must be incited among the elements by opposing forces; and this stubborn disagreement must be <term>mortified <note>original: *mortificirt*; an alchemical term for the "killing" or breaking down of a substance to prepare it for a new state of being.</note></term>, which then opens up the **bodies**. The elements of the body, however, should be separated in such a way that the generative nature remains within the **growth of the flower** <note>original: *Blume*; in alchemy, the "flower" refers to the finest, most volatile and potent part of a substance that rises during distillation.</note>. This contemplation and observation of the <term>philosophers <note>original: *Philosophorum*; referring to the ancient and medieval alchemical authorities.</note></term> is precisely and truly so. But in the event that someone, out of their own fantasy, wished to invent something else, they would be a natural fool; because they would be arguing falsely or engaging in <term>sophistry <note>original: *sophisticirt*; the use of clever but false arguments.</note></term> against nature.

WHEN the ancient, world-renowned philosopher <note>original: *Philosophus*</note>, Pythagoras of Samos, accepted new incoming disciples to be instructed in his college <note>original: *Collegium*</note>, it is said that he laid this command upon them above all things: that no one should gossip about the lessons <note>original: *lectionibus*</note> they were undertaking outside of the school. For that reason, every one of his listeners <note>original: *Auditorer*</note> had to remain as if mute for five years; so much so, that they were permitted neither to ask their master and preceptor <note>original: *Præceptorem*</note> the slightest question about the things they heard and learned, nor to speak a single word among themselves or discourse upon them. This custom was kept by the successors of Pythagoras, until finally—because memory is weak—they began [to write down] that which they had learned from their preceptor, concerning both the first original main sources of all things, which are called the Principles <term>Principia: Referring here to the *Principia rerum*, the fundamental building blocks or "first principles" from which all matter in the universe is derived.</term>

## Chapter XVIII.

### Demonstrating that the Stone possesses the power and effect to cure all diseases and restore health, for all of nature exists entirely within the Sun, and the Sun within nature; and especially within the Stone.

# Of the Philosopher’s Stone.

file it finely; add it to the Mercury, according to the second proportion against the <term>value of the Moon (original: *precio Lunæ*; alchemical shorthand for silver)</term>. Set it over a gentle fire; continue with this so long until, in the Mercury—which dissolves the bodies—a sulfur floating on top appears: draw this out, until nothing of the body remains. And thus you have the first part of the Philosophical Work.

The second part is this: Place the sulfur in a glass without water; and the body's Mercurial Water—in which its Mercurial soul is—you shall gently distill. Add this water to the sulfur and mix it together, so that often and many times one with the other, now rising above, now sinking below <note>This describes the process of "circulation" or refluxing, where vapors rise and condense back into the matter.</note>, until the sulfur has received its water, which happens in the whitest color, like snow. And thus you have an Elixir or medicine, prepared in this way.

The third part of this work is this: When you now have the whitest earth, then make it yellow-colored in a strong fire; thereafter make it with force, with a greater fire, entirely red. And this is an Elixir or <term>tincture for the red (original: *Tinctur ad rubeum*; the final stage of the alchemical work used to create gold)</term>.

### operate.

This Divine Art, it pleases us to grasp with even shorter words, yet with wondrous profoundness.

Dissolve the body: Take the sulfur, cleanse it of its impurity; sublime the spirit

# Of the Philosopher’s Stone.

and add it to the sulfur. In this way, you possess the Philosophical Art. In every perfect work of <term>Alchemy (original: *Alchymiæ*)</term>, however small it may be, it is highly necessary to have the spirit and the sulfur. The spirit tinges with the color of gold; the sulfur provides the weight of gold and <term>coagulates (original: *coagulirt*; turns from liquid to solid)</term>. If one of these is missing from the work, you will accomplish nothing. The philosophers seek the whole secret of nature in the sulfur or "earth" of gold, in which it lies hidden, and they say it is entirely true. Therefore, they call it a <term>coagulum (original: *Coagulum*; a thickening or curdling agent)</term>, or hardening, when they say: Take the *coagulum* or hardening from the body, and you have the true <term>magisterium (original: *Magisterium*; the 'mastery' or completed work of the art)</term>, or the mastery of the art, above which there is nothing greater or higher in nature. Similarly: Purify the *coagulum* and extinguish its <note>The original term *Hinternussen* literally means "back-nuts," a metaphorical way of saying "hindrances" or "obstacles."</note> hindrances, and you will <term>tinge (original: *tingiren*; to dye or transform metal)</term> whatever you wish. However, our sulfur is compared to an unclean cloth, which cannot be purified without water: likewise, our "earthly" sulfur is not washed without its water. To wash is to dissolve; to dissolve is to purify. The water is the <term>Mercury (original: *Mercurius*)</term>; this is the key which alone unlocks the body and makes the sulfur white; if the key is not present, the impurity will not be removed.

I shall regard, hold, and praise you—or whoever it may be—as a man endowed with a singular skill, if you can remove that same impurity. This very thing is the hindrance/
